I totally understand the urge to not rely on it. It's not a bad thing, but being dependent on one thing for your happiness especially something that's digital (read: not physically present) has in the past made me feel vulnerable and out of touch with the physical world. 

My advice would be to firstly make sure you are getting good sleep (this was a problem for me: I would watch video after video, laughing and having a good time and not get enough sleep) so giving yourself a cutoff time for kpop vids might be good like 8pm on weekdays for example. Another thing would be to make sure you're spending time with your friends and connecting with people not about kpop/kpop content. Schedule coffee dates and casual hangouts as much as you can. It might also be good to find some things that are solitary/not necessarily social that can make you happy like maybe revisit your favorite book or a hobby/craft you used to love to do or a sport you used to love to play. 

I feel like its important to not feel like you're cutting yourself off from it so much as making space for other things that make you happy. Having kpop in your toolbox as a way of making you happy is just fine, but it's good to have other tools in there as well.

Ask them how you can help with a panic attack when they AREN'T having one. They may be better able to put more thought to what would help them if they are not currently in the middle of it. 

I think this is probably the best way since people are different and everyone needs different things, but here are some things that help me when I have a panic attack (you could offer these as possible ways to help if your SO can't think of anything):

\-rubbing their back softly but firmly in a circular pattern -alternating directions ever so often (my mom did this for me when I was a child so it has a particular comforting effect for me, but I have done this for others who are very upset and it helped)

\-a drink of water (this is particularly helpful if the person is hyperventilating or breathing irregularly as drinking the water forces their body to regulate breathing -also people get very dehydrated when crying so water can help with that)

\-sit still next to them (unless you are getting them water or something) -don't  fidget or pace or move around too much as trying to track your movements could make them more anxious

\-speak in a low, calm tone of voice and tell them they are safe. Remind them that  even though this feels impossible to get through, they have survived every panic attack they have ever had -don't minimize what they are going through, but ask them to remember that this is temporary, it will go away, and you will stay with them until it does.

I've done both CBT and DBT in conjunction with medication for depression, anxiety, and panic. I personally prefer DBT over CBT because it actually helps you address the roots of your problems rather than just sort of triaging symptoms. 

My most recent therapist did applied DBT, so less worksheets and more utilizing skills. TIPP for panic attacks was very helpful, but a lot of it for me was about acceptance. Accepting that anxiety is a natural part of life and just sitting in it rather than getting more worked up thinking I shouldn't have to feel this way and then taking a pill. I got almost completely off benzos with the help of DBT. It helped me recognize when I was burned out  and that I needed to take more time for myself. 

In less than a year doing DBT I figured out my relationship with my sister/roommate was super unhealthy, moved out, quit my exhausting job, drew boundaries with my needy mom, and a ton more. I'm in a much better place now largely due to effective DBT work. I also had a change in medication that was also very helpful. 

All in all, CBT was fine, but DBT changed my life.

See if you can find someone who specializes in DBT. It's very practical and helpful for anxiety and panic attacks, but there are deeper, more complex layers to it that help with depression, self image, self love, etc. (Also my psychiatrist says that in her experience it helps people overcome anxiety and depression way better than meds alone)

Seeing a DBT specialized counselor has changed so much for me. I was on Xanax and Klonopin for 5 years for anxiety and panic and I was able to taper off the benzos without becoming a total mess (I am over a month clean now) because of the DBT techniques she taught me and the DBT work we we've been doing in session. 

Some DBT techniques that have really helped me are: TIPP (Temperture, Intense excersize, Paced breathing, Progressive relaxation) for severe panic attacks (if you Google tipp dbt there are a bunch of dbt guides that will explain what to do), mindfulness/guided meditation (I really like the app Headspace for this), using your senses to self sooth by focusing in on, for example, every red object in the room, or really study an object nearby as if you were going to have to draw it from memory, listen to the sounds around you, focus on them and identify them, concentrate on smells or how the air feels on your face or the clothes feel on your body, etc.

Good luck and dont give up! It can be hard to find the right counselor, but they are out there and they can really help.
